articles.title: The UK's new ISSB-based sustainability reporting rules for listed companies - Freshfields
articles.summary: The UK's new ISSB-based sustainability reporting rules for listed companies  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
This blog was originally published on 3 February 2026 and updated on 8 October 2026.
The UK’s new sustainability reporting listing rules have been finalised, replacing TCFD with the UK sustainability reporting standards (UK SRS), and will apply to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Details are set out in the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)’s newly-published Policy Statement PS26/19. The objective of the new rules and the UK SRS is to align sustainability reporting by listed companies with the global baseline set by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) (which has subsumed TCFD), and with investor demand for relevant and robust disclosures.
Under the final listing rules, the new UK SRS reporting standards will apply on a "comply or explain" basis across the same five in-scope listing categories as the current TCFD-based rules. All obligations will apply on a "comply or explain" basis. As noted above, the rules apply to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, so the first reports will be published in 2028 – however, the inclusion of transitional relief to defer reporting on wider sustainability topics under UK SRS S1 by two years (to 1 January 2029), means that reporting on the 2027 financial year will be limited to climate reporting under UK SRS S2. There is also a transitional relief allowing the deferral of reporting on Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions by one year (to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2028).
The final rules are both lighter and broader than the regime set out in the FCA’s January – March 2026 consultation, under which S2 climate disclosures were proposed to be mandatory, save that companies with a secondary listing or depositary receipts were permitted to comply by signposting their home-jurisdiction reporting. Listed companies should also be aware that there is a draft Technical Note included in the FCA’s Policy Statement, linked above, which set out examples of reporting, and guidance on how the “comply or explain” principles should be interpretated in practice. This draft is open for consultation until 28 October 2026.
This blog outlines who is in scope, what will change, how the rules evolved from the consultation, how the UK's approach compares internationally, and what companies should be doing now to prepare.
Who will report what and when?
The FCA will replace the sustainability reporting requirements in the current listing rules, based on the recommendations of the near-obsolete Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), with the new UK SRS. These new standards are derived from the work of the ISSB, which was launched formally at COP26 in Glasgow and which aims to establish a single global baseline for reporting. Like the existing TCFD listing rules, the FCA's UK SRS rules apply in largely the same way to companies in the commercial, non-equity and transition categories and issuers with a secondary listing or depositary receipts (around 570 issuers across the five categories, based on the FCA’s Official List as at 2 October 2026).
Obligations are imposed on these listed companies (whether or not incorporated in the UK) to prepare and publish disclosures addressing their "reporting entity", which is defined in paragraph 20 of UK SRS S1 as having the same scope as the group addressed by their consolidated financial statements.
In-scope companies will be required to include the following in their annual financial report:
From 2027: climate disclosures. For accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, disclosures against UK SRS S2 (other than Scope 3 emissions) replace the current TCFD-aligned disclosures, on the same “comply or explain” basis. A company that does not make some or all of the disclosures must summarise the requirements it has not met, explain why, and set out any steps it is taking or plans to take to make them in future. The FCA had consulted on making these disclosures mandatory but concluded that, given feedback that full disclosure “is not yet feasible for certain smaller issuers”, a mandatory approach “may be disproportionately burdensome for small companies”.
From 2028: Scope 3 emissions. A one-year transitional relief means that Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions – the indirect greenhouse gas emissions that occur across a company's entire value chain – come within the “comply or explain” regime for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2028.
From 2029: wider sustainability topics. A two-year “climate-first” relief means that disclosures on wider, non-climate sustainability topics under UK SRS S1 come within the “comply or explain” regime for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2029. A company that has not identified any relevant sustainability-related risks or opportunities must say so. A company relying on either relief must state this in its annual financial report, but no further explanation is needed during the relief period. Early adopters can use the reliefs again for their first accounting period beginning on or after 1 January 2027.
Transition plan and assurance statements. From 2027, statements setting out where in the annual financial report the UK SRS disclosures can be found, whether any of them have been independently assured (and, if so, by whom, which disclosures, to what level and against which standards), and whether the company has published a climate transition plan (and, if so, where it can be found or, if not, why not). Neither assurance nor a transition plan is itself mandatory, although the FCA will keep the case for mandatory assurance under review. The transition plan statement does not apply to companies with a secondary listing or depositary receipts.
Bringing secondary-listed companies into the full regime is the most striking change from the proposal set out in the consultation. To support the international competitiveness of UK markets, the FCA had originally proposed a much lighter-touch approach – just explaining what sustainability disclosure requirements apply in their primary jurisdiction, any voluntary standards that they adopt, and where those disclosures can be found. That proposal did not survive consultation. Some respondents warned that it would let issuers from jurisdictions with no sustainability reporting requirements disclose nothing and might even tempt UK companies to downgrade to a secondary listing or use depositary receipts to sidestep the full regime. The final rules instead mirror the current approach to TCFD: where home-jurisdiction reporting aligns with the outcomes of UK SRS, these issuers may rely on it to reduce duplication, but they must explain any gaps.
How the UK compares internationally
Globally, regulators outside of the EU are converging around the ISSB Standards: the IFRS Foundation, as of 24 September 2026, has identified 37 jurisdictions that have adopted, or are moving to adopt, them, although approaches to implementation differ. The FCA said in consultation that it wanted to balance investor needs with the practical readiness of companies; its policy statement cites “proportionality, market readiness and UK competitiveness concerns”. In practice, that means giving UK issuers more flexibility than many other jurisdictions, particularly on Scope 3 and wider S1-type disclosures, and now on climate disclosures too.
The UK has adopted a “comply or explain” approach to climate and wider sustainability disclosures under UK SRS S1 and S2 that allows companies to explain their reporting gaps as they build up their data capabilities. Other jurisdictions are taking different paths: Hong Kong already requires climate reporting from its largest issuers and plans to extend this to full S1- and S2-aligned reporting by 2028, while Singapore's ISSB-based requirements cover climate only and so far apply just to Straits Times Index constituents, with other listed issuers following from FY2028 or FY2030. The EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) already requires broader sustainability disclosures – where material – under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), although the Omnibus I Directive has narrowed the scope and delayed some elements, and simplified ESRS will apply from 2027. Australia, by contrast, is focusing initially on climate reporting with voluntary S1-type disclosures, while New Zealand’s climate standards remain TCFD-based, although its standard setter has proposed moving to an IFRS S2-based standard, harmonised with Australia and mandatory from 2033.
There are also variations in how each of these countries has applied reporting obligations to corporate groups. For example, Australia requires global groups to extract and publish information specific to Australian group entities, whilst other countries are considering allowing local subsidiaries to meet reporting requirements by cross-referencing global group reports. It remains to be seen how the UK will apply UK SRS reporting to private companies who are part of broader global groups, as these rules only address listed companies, who are invariably ultimate parents.
Approaches to Scope 3 reporting also vary across jurisdictions. In the EU, Scope 3 is required to be measured and disclosed under CSRD where material, and the simplified ESRS give it no phase-in of its own. The Omnibus I Directive, in force from March 2026 (see our summary), reduces the number of companies in scope but retains the requirement for those still covered. Australia has legislated for mandatory Scope 3 reporting from an entity's second reporting year, meaning Group 1 entities must disclose for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026, supported by a modified liability regime protecting Scope 3 disclosures from private claims for financial years beginning before 2028. articles.full_text:
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners Invests in 20 Italian Biomethane Projects
- Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has approved its first investment through Advanced Bioenergy Fund II, entering Italy’s growing biomethane market.
- The Via Verde platform comprises 20 projects across Italy, with planned annual production of approximately 1 TWh of renewable gas.
- The investment will strengthen domestic energy supply, reduce reliance on imported fossil gas and support Italy’s 2030 biomethane targets.
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has reached a final investment decision on Via Verde, an Italian biomethane platform comprising 20 development projects. The investment expands CIP’s European renewable energy portfolio and establishes its presence in Italy’s emerging renewable gas sector.
The transaction, executed through CIP’s Advanced Bioenergy Fund II (ABF II), is the fund’s first investment. Financial terms were not disclosed.
Via Verde will convert agricultural waste into biomethane, providing a domestic alternative to imported fossil gas. The platform aims to support Italy’s energy security while advancing national decarbonisation objectives.
Once fully operational, the projects are expected to produce approximately 1 terawatt-hour (TWh) of biomethane annually. That volume is equivalent to the annual gas consumption of around 60,000 Italian households.
Building Italy’s Domestic Biomethane Capacity
Via Verde comprises 20 projects distributed across several Italian regions, including Lombardy, Abruzzo and Campania.
Each facility is expected to process between 60,000 and 100,000 tonnes of agricultural waste annually. Across the portfolio, this represents potential processing capacity of 1.2 million to 2 million tonnes per year.
The facilities will transform agricultural residues and other sustainable feedstocks into renewable gas suitable for replacing fossil-based natural gas.
Biomethane offers a potential decarbonisation pathway for sectors that continue to depend on gaseous fuels. Its compatibility with existing gas infrastructure can also reduce the need for extensive network modifications.
For Italy, expanding domestic biomethane production carries additional strategic importance. The country remains dependent on imported natural gas, leaving energy consumers exposed to international supply disruptions and price volatility.
Locally produced renewable gas could help diversify supply while creating employment opportunities in agricultural communities.
CIP Targets Growth in European Renewable Gas
ABF II focuses on developing, constructing and operating biogas facilities across Europe.
The fund targets projects that convert agricultural waste and other sustainable feedstocks into biomethane, supporting renewable energy production and circular resource management.
Via Verde provides CIP with an initial platform in Italy, where national energy policies and renewable gas incentives are encouraging investment.
Andreas F. Brandt, Partner at CIP, said: “Via Verde marks our entry into one of Europe’s most attractive biomethane markets, giving us a strong foothold as Italy scales towards its 2030 biomethane targets. CIP will leverage its advanced bioenergy expertise to support Via Verde’s experienced local team and substantial project pipeline, laying a strong foundation for long-term growth. We believe biomethane will play a key role in strengthening Italy’s energy independence and supporting its transition to a lower-carbon energy system.”
CIP expects to combine its advanced bioenergy investment experience with Via Verde’s local development capabilities.
The platform’s regional footprint also offers opportunities to establish agricultural feedstock supply chains and expand production capacity over time.
RELATED ARTICLE: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners Raises Record €12 Billion for Energy Transition Infrastructure Fund
Policy Support Drives Investment Opportunities
Italy has identified biomethane as an important component of its energy transition strategy, particularly for reducing fossil gas consumption.
National support mechanisms and European Union energy policies are helping create more favourable conditions for renewable gas investment.
The EU’s REPowerEU strategy targets annual biomethane production of 35 billion cubic metres by 2030, reflecting the bloc’s efforts to diversify energy supplies.
For infrastructure investors, these policy commitments create opportunities to finance renewable gas assets with long-term production potential.
However, project economics remain dependent on feedstock availability, operating costs, regulatory stability and access to appropriate infrastructure.
Sustainable sourcing will also be important as biomethane production expands. Agricultural waste utilisation must deliver measurable emissions reductions without creating additional environmental pressures.
Implications for European Energy Investment
Via Verde adds to growing institutional investment in renewable gas infrastructure as European governments pursue energy security and climate objectives.
For investors, the platform offers exposure to an emerging infrastructure segment supported by decarbonisation policies and demand for domestically produced energy.
Its eventual contribution will depend on successful project development, construction and commercial operations.
With 20 facilities planned, CIP’s investment could help establish a substantial Italian biomethane production network.
The broader significance extends beyond Italy. Scaling commercially viable biomethane projects could provide European energy markets with another domestic supply option while supporting the transition away from fossil fuels.

articles.title: SFDR 2.0: Parliament adopts its negotiating mandate as trilogues get the green light, Premlata Fagan - Linklaters - Sustainable Futures
articles.summary: SFDR 2.0: Parliament adopts its negotiating mandate as trilogues get the green light, Premlata Fagan  Linklaters - Sustainable Futures
articles.full_text:
In the latest stage on the journey of SFDR 2.0 through the EU legislative process, the European Parliament's ECON Committee has adopted its report on the review of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation and approved the mandate to open trilogue negotiations with the Council. Parliament has now announced its mandate, with the first trilogue meeting between Parliament, Council and the Commission expected to take place shortly in October. Co-legislators are aiming to reach political agreement by the end of 2026, with formal adoption and publication in the Official Journal to follow; based on an anticipated 18 to 24-month transition period, the rules are expected to go live at the end of 2028 or in early 2029.
Overall, Parliament broadly supports the Commission's three-category product framework (Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics) and the architecture around it, but introduces a number of targeted adjustments – most notably on fossil fuel exposures, Taxonomy-alignment thresholds and the treatment of public-sector debt. On a number of the most contested points, the amendments adopted by ECON move Parliament's position materially closer to the Council's negotiating mandate of 24 June 2026 (including proposals to increase the implementation period to 2 years, include an opt-out for AIFs marketed only to Per Se Professionals and proposals around grandfathering of existing closed funds, and ramp up periods for Article 7,8,9 products to meet the 70% eligible investment threshold) which should help narrow the scope of the trilogue discussions to focus on key areas of divergence.
Key points of Parliament's mandate
- Three-category framework confirmed. Parliament endorses the Commission's architecture built around Transition (Art. 7), ESG Basics (Art. 8) and Sustainable (Art. 9) products. In line with the Commission draft, products in each category must disclose their PAIs, with additional safeguards aimed at preventing greenwashing.
- Transition category – tighter fossil fuel gating. Parliament adopts a more restrictive approach than the Council for fossil fuel-related exposures. To qualify, fossil fuel companies must allocate at least 20% of CapEx to Taxonomy-aligned activities, have a Paris Agreement-aligned emissions reduction plan and, where relevant, maintain a time-bound coal phase-out strategy. In addition, qualifying companies must, over a rolling three-year period, allocate a greater share of CapEx to Taxonomy-aligned activities than to new fossil fuel expansion.
- Higher Taxonomy threshold for Sustainable products. Unlike the Council, which applies a single 15% Taxonomy-alignment threshold to both the Sustainable and Transition categories, Parliament requires 20% Taxonomy alignment for Sustainable products while maintaining 15% for Transition products – a point of divergence that will need to be reconciled in trilogues.
- Public-sector bonds – partially accommodated. Parliament allows general-purpose public-sector bonds to contribute towards the Transition category threshold, subject to specific conditions and capped at 15 percentage points. Such instruments remain excluded from the Sustainable category, which is reserved for use-of-proceeds instruments such as green bonds. The 15-percentage-point cap for the Transition category broadly aligns with the approach taken by the Council.
- Targeted simplification measures. Parliament aligns with the Council on a 24-month application period following entry into force, but proposes that the removal of certain entity-level disclosures – including principal adverse impact statements and remuneration-related disclosures – should apply immediately on entry into force in order to accelerate reporting-burden relief.
Next steps
The first trilogue meeting is scheduled for later this month (perhaps as early as 13th October). Co-legislators are targeting political agreement by the end of 2026, after which the text will go through legal-linguistic finalisation and formal adoption by Parliament and Council before publication in the Official Journal. We will continue to track developments as the trilogue negotiations progress and will post further updates as technical and political landing zones emerge

articles.title: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology - European Rubber Journal
articles.summary: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology  European Rubber Journal
articles.full_text:
"Implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product” 
Gurugram, India – Apollo Tyres has partnered with Emertech Innovations to establish an integrated compliance and traceability system for its natural rubber (NR) supply-chain under the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
The implementation covers 56,491 source plots spanning around 150,000 hectares across India and several international sourcing markets, according to an Emertech case-study published 5 Oct.
The plot data, said the technology partner, comprises 43,932 point-based plots and 12,559 polygon-based plots within Apollo's NR supplier network.
The process involves five stages – engage; validate; assess; trace and file – each building on the one before, with an administrative portal that gives Apollo’s teams one view across all of them.
Under the system, NR suppliers submit GeoJSON files, sourcing information, risk evidence and supporting documents through a dedicated supplier portal.
The platform checks submissions for file structure, coordinates, geometry and mandatory plot information, as well as the correct use of points or polygons.
Using a satellite-based deforestation analysis tool, Emertech examines land within the submitted plot boundaries, comparing historical satellite imagery with current forest-cover and land-use information.
The analysis, it said, assesses evidence of changes after the EUDR regulatory cut-off date of 31 Dec 2020 and assigns a risk result to each plot.
The system also flags potentially risky plots which will be “held for review” before being allowed into the compliant supply-chain.
Emertech has “integrated” the compliance platform with Apollo's existing ERP and operational systems, allowing validated supplier and plot information to be linked to all supply-chain documents.
These include purchase-orders, incoming consignment notes, goods receipts, material and batch records, production transactions, finished products and export shipments.
As described by Emertech, the process maintains the connection “from the land where the NR originated to the product eventually placed on the European market.”
For EU-bound shipments, the system consolidates the applicable source-plot information and prepares the relevant due diligence statement.
Furthermore, the platform is integrated with the EU Information System within the TRACES NT environment, allowing statements to be filed directly with the EU system.
Submission status and reference numbers are subsequently returned to Apollo's central “administrative portal,” which provides “one view across every stage for compliance, procurement and operational teams.”
The portal also maintains a record linking all declarations with the suppliers, source plots, risk evidence, production records and shipment concerned.
“EUDR requires a high degree of transparency and traceability across the NR supply chain,” said Shibu George, group head, advanced manufacturing & enterprise application, at Apollo Tyres.
The collaboration with Emertech, he added, had enabled Apollo to bring together “sourcing, traceability and geospatial validation capabilities at scale,” covering a significant NR sourcing footprint.
“This implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product,” concluded George.

articles.title: PPWR: Circular economy begins in design - Label and Narrow Web
articles.summary: PPWR: Circular economy begins in design  Label and Narrow Web
articles.full_text:
Recyclability is evolving from a voluntary quality feature into a regulatory requirement. The new EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) stipulates that by 2030 all packaging must be recyclable and contain mandatory shares of post-consumer recycled material. Companies face rising requirements, higher material costs, and increasing pressure on supply chains. At the same time, circular material flows reduce dependence on primary raw materials and decrease waste generation.
The circular outcome is largely determined during the design stage. Material selection, colors, composite structures, and additives decide whether packaging can be efficiently recycled – or whether valuable resources are lost. As a result, Design for Recycling is becoming a key lever for sustainable packaging and for packaging that will remain marketable in the future.
Key Elements of the PPWR
From 2030 onwards, a binding standard will apply: all packaging must be at least 70%  materially recyclable. The EU regulation classifies packaging recyclability into three grades:
• Class A: up to 95%
• Class B: up to 80%
• Class C: up to 70% (minimum threshold)
Packaging classified as Class C will gradually be phased out of the market.
At the same time, binding quotas for post-consumer recycled mate-rials (PCR) apply to packaging design:
• PET contact-sensitive packaging: 30%
• Contact-sensitive non-PET plastics: 10%
• Single-use beverage bottles: 30%
• Other plastic packaging: 35%
By 2040, these quotas will increase depending on the category, rang-ing from 25% to up to 65%.
Recycled Materials Becoming Scarce
The PPWR could significantly increase the cost of plastic packaging. Design, manufacturing, and sourcing must be adapted to meet recy-clability criteria and mandatory recycled-content quotas. Studies therefore predict that demand for PCR could exceed available supply by around 30% .
For this reason, experts expect potential shortages of recycled plas-tics . Such bottlenecks and resulting price increases could place sig-nificant pressure on both markets and consumers.
Low-cost imports may temporarily increase the supply of recycled materials and ease price pressure. However, suppliers from coun-tries with lower environmental and labor standards – as well as lower energy costs – pose a risk to Europe’s recycling industry. Regional recyclers struggle to compete under stricter regulatory and cost structures. Investments in Design for Recycling and local recycling capacity may become less profitable, while high-quality PCR supply chains could be destabilized. The result could be de-clining material quality and growing import dependence, along with significant procurement risks.
In the long term, Design for Recycling – together with efficient col-lection systems for recyclable plastics and the development of new recycling technologies – will determine whether Europe can gener-ate sufficient high-quality post-consumer recyclate from its own material streams and establish an independent circular economy.
Preparation Is Key
The leading manufacturer of rigid plastic packaging, ALPLA, integrates recycling directly into its production processes. ALPLA CEO Philipp Lehner explains: “We integrate the entire recycling process in Europe, from bale to the production of post-consumer recyclate. We do not rely on low-cost imports.” 
With its own recycling facilities and a closed-loop approach, the company both promotes the circular economy and secures its production reliability and material quality.
The example of ALPLA demonstrates that companies investing early in Design for Recycling, high-quality PCR supply chains, and efficient recycling processes gain regulatory security, stable production sys-tems, and long-term competitiveness. 
The PPWR makes one thing clear: the circular economy does not begin at disposal – it begins in design. Companies that act consistently at this stage lay the founda-tion for sustainable success.
Source: yes or no Media GmbH

articles.title: PensionsEurope calls for greater flexibility for pension funds under SFDR 2.0 - Investment & Pensions Europe
articles.summary: PensionsEurope calls for greater flexibility for pension funds under SFDR 2.0  Investment & Pensions Europe
articles.full_text:
PensionsEurope has called on co-legislators to further loosen the rules for pension funds under the proposed update to the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR 2.0).
The trade body published its latest position on the regime, which is ready to enter political negotiations after a Parliamentary meeting this week.
It said that, while it welcomed many of the amendments suggested as part of the overhaul, more needed to be done to accommodate Europe’s pension funds.
Specifically, PensionsEurope wants SFDR 2.0 to distinguish between the way Institutions for Occupational Retirement Provision (IORPs) communicate with their members and beneficiaries, and the way financial institutions market to prospective investors.
Each of the EU’s three legislative bodies plan to ensure that pension funds – along with all other investors – are barred from making sustainability-related claims if their portfolios do not qualify for one of the regime’s three categories: ESG Basics, Transition and Sustainable.
PensionsEurope argues that member states should be allowed to remove IORPs from the SFDR categorisation framework altogether, but – given the European Council, Parliament and Commission have all taken that option off the table in their final positions – a more flexible approach should be sought instead.
Parliament will push to add a line into the legislative text allowing IORPs to communicate to their members “in a manner that fits their characteristics”.
The trade body welcomed that plan, but insisted it should “be clarified to ensure that IORPs can provide meaningful information on how sustainability factors are considered in the management of pension schemes” even if they don’t qualify for one of the categories.
Pension funds should simply have to ensure that their sustainability disclosures are “fair, clear and non-misleading,” it said.
The document also proposed the addition of a passage clarifying that pension funds do not have to double-check SFDR-related statements made by their asset managers in relation to funds run on their behalf, saying “financial market participants should be able to rely on information from underlying categorised products and regulated portfolio managers”.
Parliament confirmed on Monday that it will bypass the usual plenary vote when it comes to its negotiating position for SFDR 2.0, and is therefore ready to enter into trialogues with the European Commission and Council immediately.

articles.title: Western Balkans adopts regional frameworks for biodiversity and ecosystem restoration by 2030 - cna.al
articles.summary: Western Balkans adopts regional frameworks for biodiversity and ecosystem restoration by 2030  cna.al
articles.full_text:
The Western Balkans now have a common framework to advance in the field of biodiversity conservation and restoration of degraded ecosystems, through the adoption of two key regional frameworks: the Western Balkans Six Biodiversity Strategic Plan 2030 and the Western Balkans Six Forest Landscape Restoration Plan.
These frameworks represent an important step in implementing the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans and in aligning the region with European and global biodiversity objectives.
Both regional frameworks were adopted on 18 September 2026 in ?abljak, Montenegro, during the Third Ministerial Meeting on the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans.
Together, the plans provide a shared roadmap for conserving biodiversity, restoring ecosystems and resilience to climate change by 2030. Their key objectives include protecting at least 30% of terrestrial, freshwater, marine and coastal areas, restoring at least 20% of degraded ecosystems, halting species loss and improving ecological connectivity across the region.
The Western Balkans Six Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2030 aligns regional priorities with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030. It aims to strengthen networks of protected and conserved areas, improve biodiversity monitoring and data collection, and integrate nature conservation considerations into sectors such as agriculture, forestry, energy, 
water management and infrastructure development.
The Western Balkans Six Forest Landscape Restoration Plan promotes an integrated approach to nature restoration, which links biodiversity conservation with sustainable forest management, climate change adaptation, soil and water conservation, and disaster risk reduction. This approach supports the long-term sustainability of ecosystems and communities across the region.
“Nature knows no borders, and neither can our response to biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation be limited by them. By adopting the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2030 and the Forest Landscape Restoration Plan, the countries of the Western Balkans have demonstrated their shared commitment to coordinated action to protect nature. IUCN looks forward to continuing to work with governments, the Regional Cooperation Council (RCC) and partners to translate these regional commitments into concrete conservation and restoration measures on the ground,” said Oliver Avramoski, Director of the IUCN Regional Office for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
Both frameworks serve as key instruments for the implementation of Pillar 5 of the 
Green Agenda for the Western Balkans: Protection of Nature and Biodiversity. They 
translate international and European commitments into concrete regional measures and actions

articles.title: Finnish circular economy companies target strong expansion - PULPAPERnews.com
articles.summary: Finnish circular economy companies target strong expansion  PULPAPERnews.com
articles.full_text:
Several companies working with circular economy, reuse and resource-efficient materials have been selected among the 30 most promising businesses in Finland’s Kasvu Open growth competition.
The companies were chosen from around 180 participants in the Kasvu Open programme, according to Uusiouutiset. Selection criteria include market potential, growth prospects, the strength of the management team and the companies’ ability to deliver on their plans.
Although the businesses represent different sectors, many of their solutions reflect developments that are becoming increasingly important for the packaging industry: longer material lifecycles, greater reuse, lower waste volumes and reduced dependence on virgin raw materials.
Reuse moves closer to the packaging mainstream
Among the selected companies is Kiertoa Oy from Seinäjoki, which operates Kiertonet, a digital marketplace for used products.
Its business model is based on extending product lifetimes and keeping materials and goods in circulation for longer. Similar principles are increasingly influencing packaging strategies, particularly as producers, retailers and logistics companies look for systems that support reusable transport and sales packaging.
The shift is also being accelerated by the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR. The regulation places stronger emphasis on packaging recyclability and reusable systems. From 2030, packaging will face more detailed design-for-recycling requirements, while several categories of transport, grouped and beverage packaging will also be subject to reuse targets.
Material efficiency becomes a competitive factor
Other Kasvu Open semifinalists include Finnester Coatings, which develops fire-protection coatings for composite materials with a focus on reducing waste and resource use.
Suomen Luonnonmaalit, meanwhile, produces surface-treatment solutions based on materials including linseed oil and lime.
These companies reflect a broader industrial trend in which material efficiency, durability and recyclability are becoming increasingly important competitive factors.
For packaging producers, the direction is particularly clear. EU rules require all packaging placed on the market to be recyclable, while recyclability performance will increasingly determine whether packaging can remain on the EU market. The legislation is also designed to support higher-quality secondary raw materials that can replace virgin materials.
Growth ambitions remain high
The 30 semifinalists currently generate combined revenue of around EUR 40 million.
If their growth plans are realised, this figure could rise to more than EUR 128 million within three years, while the companies also aim to roughly double their combined workforce.
Ten finalists will be announced on 15 October. The Kasvu Open competition concludes in Jyväskylä on 28 October, when the Growth Company of the Year will be selected.
Sources: Uusiouutiset, Kasvu Open and the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation.

articles.title: SFDR 2.0: Where do we stand now and what to expect next? - Deloitte
articles.summary: SFDR 2.0: Where do we stand now and what to expect next?  Deloitte
articles.full_text:
Where do the EU Council and Parliament stand on SFDR 2.0? Both have moved away from the Commission's November 2025 proposal, but in different directions. Trialogue negotiations are expected to begin in late October 2026, with full implementation of SFDR 2.0 expected by 2029-2030.
With SFDR 2.0, Liechtenstein and Swiss financial institutions will face new compliance requirements. The new regulation will affect Swiss financial institutions that produce, market and distribute investment products in the EU or that provide financial advice to clients in the EU. This includes asset managers, wealth managers, investment managers, banks, insurance companies, and financial advisers. The new requirements will require a reclassification of products, and a review of data collection and management systems as well as current reporting process and product documentation, including marketing materials. The compliance costs will be substantial, and the operational changes will be significant.
The final shape of SFDR 2.0 is still to be determined. The Commission's proposal set the baseline for negotiations, but both the Council and Parliament have moved away from this original text.
This blog provides a summary of the latest regulatory developments.
The current legislative status
- Council position
The European Council supports the three-category framework with emphasis on operational flexibility. Key elements include a 24-month transition period, mandatory disclosure of at least three PAI indicators for Sustainable and Transition products (with flexibility to use alternatives), permission for Transition funds to invest in fossil fuel companies if at least 20% of capital expenditure is Taxonomy-aligned and a credible greenhouse gas reduction strategy exists, and an opt-out for AIFs marketed exclusively to professional clients.
- European Parliament’s ECON Committee position
The ECON Committee adopted a more stringent position proposing over 600 amendments. Key elements include mandatory disclosure of a core set of PAI indicators across all three product categories, a 20% Taxonomy alignment threshold (versus the Commission's 15%), stricter fossil fuel exclusions (including a rolling three-year comparison and exclusion of companies with more than 1% coal revenue), mandatory engagement strategy disclosure, narrower scope (entity-level disclosures limited to largest participants; financial advice removed), and annual disclosure of fund allocation by category.
- What they agree on
All three institutions agree on replacing Articles 6, 8, and 9 with three clear product categories, a 70% investment threshold for each category, and removing the Article 2(17) sustainable investment definition.
- Points open for negotiation
Despite these areas of agreement, differences remain and will be central to the Trialogue negotiations, in particular with regard to fossil fuel exposure threshold, PAI indicators to be disclosed, criteria for ESG basic products, exemption with opt-out option for AIFs marketed solely to professional investors, scope of application, application timeline, and length of the transposition period
What happens next: the Trialogue timeline
The formal negotiations between the Council, Parliament, and Commission (Trialogue) is expected to begin in late October or beginning of November. The estimated timeline is:
- October 2026: Parliament plenary vote on ECON position
- Late October/ beginning of November 2026: Trialogue negotiations commence
- Mid-2027 (estimated): Final text agreed and published
- Late 2027/Early 2028 (estimated): Entry into force
- 2029–2030 (estimated): Compliance deadline assuming a 18-24 months transition period.
These dates are indicative and subject to change as negotiations progress.
What financial institutions should be doing now
SFDR 2.0 is coming. In the Trialogue the three legislative bodies will eventually reach a compromise and financial institutions that start preparing now will be best positioned to implement efficiently and cost-effectively.
To prepare for timely compliance, financial institutions should already start to do the following:
- Map your product portfolio. Assess how your current products would be classified under the new rules and the different positions.
- Assess your data infrastructure. Evaluate your current ESG data sources, reliability, and coverage. Identify gaps and determine what changes are needed.
- Develop compliance roadmaps for both scenarios. Create detailed implementation plans for both Council-aligned and Parliament-aligned outcome.
- Inform key stakeholders. Brief your Board and senior management on SFDR 2.0 implications and the regulatory timeline.
Ready to get started? Deloitte's Sustainable Finance team can help you assess yourexposure, plan your roadmap, and navigate the transition.

articles.title: German cabinet approves EUDR administrative implementation rules - Fordaq
articles.summary: German cabinet approves EUDR administrative implementation rules  Fordaq
articles.full_text:
Germany has advanced a separate administrative implementation measure for the EUDR. Suggested cover image: Adobe Stock.
Germany’s federal cabinet approved the draft administrative regulation for national EUDR implementation on 7 October 2026, moving forward practical simplifications previously proposed for forestry and qualifying businesses.
Cabinet moves the administrative regulation forward
The German federal cabinet approved the draft General Administrative Regulation connected with Germany's implementation of the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) on 7 October 2026. The measure appeared on the cabinet's list of items adopted without debate.
The regulation is formally titled the draft General Administrative Regulation to the law implementing the EU regulation on deforestation-free products and amending the administrative regulation under Germany's Timber Trade Safeguard Act. It was submitted by the Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Regional Identity.
This development is separate from the German EUDR enforcement bill that Fordaq reported on earlier. That bill deals with national authorities, sanctions and criminal provisions. The AVV is aimed at the way the rules are administered in practice.
Draft focuses on practical simplifications
The German government had already described the AVV in August as a vehicle for practical simplifications, particularly for agriculture and forestry. Government materials identify three areas of particular relevance: relief from geodata requirements in specified cases, the possibility of collective declarations through forestry associations, and adjustments for medium and large businesses whose EUDR-covered activities represent only part of their operations.
| Area | Draft administrative approach | Why it matters | 
|---|---|---|
| Geodata | German government materials say the AVV provides for relief from geodata requirements in specified domestic primary-producer cases. | Aims to simplify information requirements for qualifying domestic producers. | 
| Collective declarations | Forestry associations may be able to submit collective declarations. | Could reduce repetitive administrative work for participating forest owners. | 
| Partly covered businesses | Adjustments are foreseen for medium and large companies where only part of the business concerns EUDR-covered commodities. | Targets mixed businesses rather than changing the underlying EU product scope. | 
| Status | Cabinet approved the draft AVV on 7 October 2026. | This is an implementation measure, distinct from Germany's separate sanctions bill. | 
The measures do not replace the underlying EUDR. The federal government's implementation page says the national package is intended to avoid creating additional obligations beyond EU law while providing a workable national enforcement framework.
Forestry associations gain particular relevance
For the German forest sector, the provision on collective declarations is one of the most practical elements. Germany has a highly fragmented private-forest ownership structure, and forestry associations already perform shared functions for groups of owners. The draft AVV is intended to allow such organisations to play a role in submitting declarations collectively.
Fordaq is not interpreting that mechanism as a blanket exemption from EUDR obligations. The precise legal conditions and the final administrative text remain important. Companies should distinguish between simplification of the process and removal of the underlying due-diligence requirements.
A follow-up to August's implementation package
The cabinet had approved Germany's separate EUDR implementation bill on 12 August. At that stage the government also said the agriculture ministry had presented the AVV draft and highlighted the planned simplifications. The 7 October cabinet decision is therefore a new procedural step rather than a new policy concept.
That is also why this story is not a duplicate of Germany's proposed EUDR sanctions framework. One concerns penalties and enforcement powers; the other concerns administrative execution and practical simplification.
What timber companies should watch
The next point to watch is the final form and formal completion of the administrative regulation, including whether the practical wording changes during the remaining process. Forest owners, forestry associations and businesses with mixed EUDR and non-EUDR activities will need to check the final conditions rather than rely only on the headline simplifications.
For importers and processors, the AVV should also be read together with the EUDR itself, EU guidance and Germany's national implementation law. Fordaq will keep the administrative regulation and the separate sanctions legislation as distinct tracks because they address different parts of compliance.

articles.title: New Metric Predicts How Much Biodiversity a Landscape Could Actually Support - Bioengineer.org
articles.summary: New Metric Predicts How Much Biodiversity a Landscape Could Actually Support  Bioengineer.org
articles.full_text:
For decades, ecologists have measured biodiversity the way an accountant audits the past: by counting what is already there. Species lists, functional-diversity indices and habitat scores all describe realised communities, the organisms that have managed to arrive, survive and reproduce in a particular place at a particular time. But a provocative new perspective published in npj Sustainable Agriculture argues that this entire measurement tradition has a structural blind spot. It cannot answer the question that farmers, policymakers and financial regulators increasingly need answered: if management changes on this landscape, how much biodiversity could it sustain? The paper, led by Christopher John Topping of Aarhus University, introduces a concept called Functional Trait Capacity, or FTC, and backs it up with a computational demonstration showing that two landscapes can look identical to every existing metric while hiding profoundly different ecological potential.
The authors trace the problem through three generations of biodiversity metrics. Species-based indices describe community composition with precision but offer no mechanism for prediction. Functional-diversity indices, which characterise the distribution of traits such as body size, feeding mode or dispersal ability within a community, still depend on inventories of species that have already been recorded. Habitat-based metrics, the third generation, replace laborious species surveys with habitat classification, dramatically improving scalability, and they now underpin global policy. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted at COP15 in December 2022, formalises habitat-based measures in its monitoring targets for 2030. England’s mandatory Biodiversity Net Gain requirement, in force since 2024 under the Environment Act 2021, calculates standardised biodiversity units from habitat distinctiveness and condition. Yet the evidence for these proxies is sobering: studies show the English metric is associated with measurable gains in plant biodiversity but not in birds or butterflies, and it predicts invertebrate biodiversity poorly.
The deeper issue, the authors contend, is that all three metric generations measure patterns rather than the processes that generate them. Even the ambitious European Biodiversity Observation Network roadmap, with its 84 Essential Biodiversity Variables spanning genes to ecosystems, remains observational by design. Such systems can standardise how biodiversity state and change are measured, but they cannot supply the causal prediction needed to evaluate an individual management decision. Correlative models fitted to observed occurrences project associations between recorded species and recorded conditions, with the projected species pool bounded by the region and period used for fitting. They output expected occurrence, not the conditions required for persistence, and they cannot identify which ecological constraint prevents a management response. The distinction the authors draw is not between description and prediction, but between observation-anchored prediction and mechanistic prediction.
The empirical motivation for FTC comes from a stubborn and poorly explained pattern in two decades of agri-environment research: the same intervention produces different, sometimes opposite, biodiversity responses in different landscape contexts. Meta-analyses indicate that organic farming increases species richness by roughly 30 percent on average relative to conventional management, yet 16 percent of studies report negative effects. Benefits tend to be greater in intensively managed, structurally homogeneous landscapes than in heterogeneous ones. A global analysis of 60 crops across six continents confirmed that ecological benefits were greatest in intensive agricultural landscapes, while the same landscape variable could have contrasting effects on different sustainability outcomes. Agri-environment schemes show the same context dependence: a landmark five-country study found substantial variation among countries, taxa and scheme types, with common species benefiting more than species of conservation concern, and a subsequent meta-analysis showed that species richness increased in simple cropland landscapes but not in complex ones.
Spatially explicit modelling offers independent support for a capacity-based interpretation. Across 611 simulated landscapes, landscape structure explained 84 percent of variation in mean beetle density and 70 percent of variation in pesticide impact, with mitigation effects also strongly landscape dependent. The authors argue that these variable outcomes are unlikely to be failures of intervention design. Instead, an intervention acts on biodiversity capacity, a property generated by the landscape as a system, whereas evaluation usually records species occurrence at particular places and times. A predictive metric must represent the processes that generate capacity, not only the patterns those processes have already produced.
So what exactly is Functional Trait Capacity? The authors define it as the range of viable functional-trait combinations that a landscape can sustain, given specified landscape configuration, management regime and assessment horizon. The object of measurement shifts from the community currently observed to the breadth of ecological strategies and life-history solutions for which the landscape provides viable conditions. A wider trait space can support a greater range of species and functional groups, because landscapes act on the resources, disturbance regimes and environmental constraints that filter trait combinations; species composition is one historically contingent outcome of that filtering. The concept builds on Hutchinson’s classic n-dimensional hypervolume and on modern functional-trait ecology, joining them by asking which trait combinations a landscape can sustain rather than which happen to be present.
The framework distinguishes three capacity states. Theoretical FTC is the capacity expected from a site’s physical characteristics and natural ecological trajectory in the absence of deliberate management, a declared reference rather than an absolute biophysical maximum. Management-determined FTC is the capacity produced by a specified land-use and management regime, and it is not necessarily lower than the reference: management can create conditions absent from the natural trajectory, for example by maintaining open habitat where woodland would otherwise develop. Realised biodiversity is the community currently present after historical filtering, the state measured by existing metrics. The gaps between these states represent biodiversity debts or opportunities, separating capacity lost or created through management from capacity that is viable but not yet realised. Crucially, FTC is designed to complement, not replace, observational systems: monitoring tracks realised state and trend, while FTC asks the adjacent causal question of what functional capacity specified conditions should produce.
To show the concept is calculable, the team built a deterministic demonstration using 80 virtual strategies generated from 16 archetypes defined by trophic role, fast–slow life history and disturbance response. Four traits determine viability: spatial access, temporal resource requirement, disturbance tolerance and biotic dependency, with rules for phenological overlap and acyclic food-web structure excluding biologically arbitrary combinations. Four 50-by-50-cell agricultural landscapes varied field configuration and non-crop area in a two-by-two design. The striking result: the researchers selected the same 32-strategy realised community in all four landscapes, yet full assessment of all 80 admissible strategies gave FTC values of 46, 67, 44 and 65. Identical observed richness concealed a difference of up to 23 viable strategies, strategies that occur in none of the observations and therefore could never be recovered by a model fitted only to them. When the same intervention, converting 5 percent of cropped cells to semi-natural habitat along field edges, was applied everywhere, FTC rose by 14 strategies in one landscape, four in another, and not at all in the remaining two, even though mean viable area increased in every case.
Robustness analyses suggest the pattern is not an artefact. Across 60 combinations of persistence thresholds, conversion intensities and placement rules, the high-non-crop landscape always had greater FTC than its low-non-crop counterpart, and intervention effects differed among landscapes in 50 of 60 combinations. In sensitivity ensembles varying the sampled strategies and seasonal resource profiles, baseline FTC differed among landscapes in every replicate, and the intervention response differed among landscapes in all 20 combined replicates. The authors are careful about what this proves: the demonstration shows FTC can be calculated, not that it is empirically valid. Observations remain essential to parameterise resource use, movement and disturbance responses, to test predicted viability and to estimate uncertainty. Their role changes rather than disappears, informing and testing the ecological processes that the model then uses to predict viable strategies under conditions not yet observed.
The path to operational use runs through existing infrastructure. The authors envisage a process-based estimation layer supplying maps, scenario contrasts, limiting-factor diagnoses and uncertainty-bounded indicators to advisers, conservation managers and policy analysts, who would never need to run the underlying model. Inputs correspond to established data streams: Integrated Administration and Control System records for cropping, remote sensing and habitat inventories for configuration, and open trait compilations. articles.title: Nordic Development Fund, Partners Develop Climate and Peace Investment Fund
articles.summary:

articles.full_text:
Nordic Development Fund, Partners Develop Climate and Peace Investment Fund
- Five development and investment organisations are collaborating to develop a new impact investment strategy targeting climate resilience and peacebuilding in lower-income and conflict-affected countries.
- The Climate and Peace Investment Fund (CPIF) aims to expand financing for entrepreneurs creating jobs, strengthening local economies and addressing climate-related vulnerabilities.
- Public, philanthropic and private investors will be brought together to mobilise capital, with country-specific assessments guiding investment decisions and managing conflict-related risks.
The Nordic Development Fund (NDF), Incofin Investment Management, the Peace Dividend Initiative (PDI), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Switzerland’s development cooperation agency are developing a new investment strategy linking climate finance with peacebuilding.
The proposed Climate and Peace Investment Fund (CPIF) will target entrepreneurs operating in lower-income countries and conflict-affected regions. Its objective is to expand access to capital for businesses that strengthen climate resilience while supporting economic stability and social cohesion.
The initiative comes as rising conflict and worsening climate pressures place growing strain on vulnerable communities. Food insecurity, water scarcity and displacement are increasing competition for resources, particularly in regions already facing political instability.
Mobilising Climate Finance in Conflict-Affected Markets
CPIF seeks to address a persistent financing gap in markets where climate vulnerability and conflict overlap.
Entrepreneurs in these regions often face significant barriers to investment, despite operating businesses that provide employment, essential services and economic opportunities.
The fund’s proposed strategy will support enterprises that contribute to climate adaptation while helping communities build more stable livelihoods.
For investors, the initiative introduces an approach that considers both environmental outcomes and the economic conditions needed to sustain peace.
Isabel Leroux, Program Manager at Nordic Development Fund, said: “One of NDF’s priorities is to ensure that climate finance reaches the communities most vulnerable to climate change, which are too often underserved by existing financing models. By supporting CPIF from an early stage and working alongside our partners, we are helping to build the foundations for a credible investment strategy that can unlock capital at scale in lower-income countries and conflict-affected contexts, where access to climate finance remains far too limited.”
The collaboration reflects growing interest in directing climate investment towards fragile markets that conventional financing mechanisms frequently overlook.
Country-Level Assessments to Guide Investment Strategy
Over the coming months, the five organisations will undertake a comprehensive design process to develop CPIF into an investable strategy.
Country-specific assessments will identify opportunities where private enterprise can advance climate action while contributing to peacebuilding and social cohesion.
These analyses will also examine potential investment risks, including unintended consequences that could worsen existing tensions.
Such safeguards are particularly important in conflict-affected environments, where unequal access to resources and economic opportunities can intensify local grievances.
The partners intend to incorporate these considerations into the fund’s investment approach before capital deployment.
A broader coalition of public, philanthropic and private investors will also be assembled to support the initiative.
The organisations have not disclosed a target fund size, initial capital commitments or an investment launch date.
RELATED ARTICLE: IFAD Raises $72 Million Through Sustainable Bond to Fund Rural Development
Supporting Entrepreneurs as Drivers of Economic Stability
The proposed fund places local entrepreneurship at the centre of its climate and peacebuilding strategy.
Businesses operating in fragile markets can provide employment, maintain essential economic activity and create alternatives to displacement.
Their ability to adapt to climate pressures also has implications for regional food security, resource management and long-term economic resilience.
Liam Foran, CEO of the Peace Dividend Initiative, said: “PDI’s experience is that local entrepreneurs have innovative solutions to adapt to climate change, what they often lack is capital. This is especially the case in countries emerging from conflict. By working with our partners to launch the CPIF, PDI aims to harness capital at scale to support entrepreneurs in frontier markets.”
The initiative aims to connect these enterprises with financing sources that have historically struggled to reach fragile and underserved economies.
Implications for Global Climate and Impact Investors
CPIF’s development raises broader questions about how climate finance can operate effectively in politically unstable environments.
For institutional and impact investors, the proposed strategy could provide a framework for assessing climate outcomes alongside conflict sensitivity and social impact.
Its success will depend on attracting sufficient capital, identifying commercially viable enterprises and establishing credible safeguards against unintended harm.
The approach also aligns with international efforts to improve climate finance access for vulnerable developing economies.
By combining development finance expertise, private investment management and peacebuilding experience, the partners aim to expand the range of investable opportunities in frontier markets.
For global investors, CPIF could offer a model for financing climate resilience in regions where environmental vulnerability and political instability increasingly intersect. Its eventual scale and effectiveness will depend on the investment structure that emerges from the design process.

articles.title: Shell Foundation Backs $200 Million Climate Finance Fund for Emerging Markets
articles.summary:
Shell Foundation and the UK government are backing a $200 million climate finance fund designed to mobilise private investment into clean transportation and energy businesses across emerging markets. The Lendable […]

articles.full_text:
Shell Foundation Backs $200 Million Climate Finance Fund for Emerging Markets
- Shell Foundation and the UK government anchor Lendable’s Transportation and Energy Fund, using first-loss capital to attract institutional and private investment into emerging markets.
- The fund secured $135 million at its first close, targeting $200 million by mid-2027 to finance clean transportation, renewable energy and underserved enterprises.
- Initial investments support electric mobility in Africa and rural solar financing in India, expanding access to credit while reducing emissions and supporting economic inclusion.
Shell Foundation and the UK government are backing a $200 million climate finance fund designed to mobilise private investment into clean transportation and energy businesses across emerging markets.
The Lendable Transportation and Energy Fund (LTEF) secured $135 million at its first close in December 2025. It aims to reach $200 million by mid-2027.
Shell Foundation’s cornerstone investment, supported by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), provides the fund’s first-loss capital. The structure reduces exposure for other investors, helping attract institutional finance into underserved markets.
The investment builds on nearly a decade of collaboration between Shell Foundation and Lendable, a technology-enabled investment firm managing more than $1 billion in assets under advisory.
Catalytic Capital Attracts Institutional Investment
Shell Foundation’s investment anchors LTEF’s most junior tranche, absorbing initial losses before senior investors face exposure.
This blended finance approach combines philanthropic, public and private capital to support commercially viable climate investments.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), FMO, SIFEM and several family offices are among the fund’s other investors. They are anchoring its senior and Class A tranches.
Shell Foundation initially supported Lendable in 2016 through grant funding for its credit assessment and data infrastructure. LTEF is its first direct investment into a Lendable-managed fund.
Lendable uses its proprietary Maestro platform to assess credit risk, monitor assets and verify financial and impact performance.
Nick Jones, Head of Financial Solutions at Shell Foundation, said:
“Too many businesses delivering climate solutions in emerging markets struggle to access the financing they need to scale, despite strong demand and clear potential to improve livelihoods while reducing emissions. By anchoring the Lendable Transportation and Energy Fund, we are helping to demonstrate how catalytic capital can unlock significantly larger pools of private investment into sectors that are critical to an inclusive low-carbon transition. We hope this signals to the market that climate-focused businesses serving underserved communities can deliver both meaningful impact and attractive investment opportunities.”
Electric Mobility Financing Expands Across Africa
LTEF’s first transaction supports Watu, an asset financing company operating across Africa and Latin America.
Watu has financed more than 8,000 electric vehicles since expanding into electric mobility in 2021.
The fund’s investment will help scale its lease-to-own electric motorcycle business to approximately 1,000 vehicles monthly.
The financing targets commercial riders who depend on motorcycles for income generation, while supporting lower-emission transportation.
Lendable has partnered with Watu since 2017, providing financing expertise as the company expanded across multiple emerging markets.

$5 Million Facility Supports Rural Solar Adoption in India
LTEF’s second investment provides a $5 million facility to Metafin, an Indian lender financing solar photovoltaic systems for rural enterprises.
Metafin operates through more than 700 local solar installation partners across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
The company has financed over 6,500 solar systems. The new facility will support another 1,300 enterprises.
Lendable estimates the investment will avoid approximately 11,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent over the loans’ lifetimes.
Financial inclusion is another priority. Approximately 46% of Metafin’s customers are accessing formal credit for the first time, while 49% of loans include a female co-applicant.
Closing the Emerging Market Climate Finance Gap
Daniel Goldfarb, Executive Chairman and Co-founder of Lendable, highlighted the scale of unmet investment demand:
“There is a critical gap between the capital emerging markets need to decarbonise and the capital currently flowing to them. Asia alone requires an estimated $1.3 trillion a year, while Africa receives just around a quarter of its financing needs. For investors, that gap represents one of the more compelling opportunities in private markets today. LTEF’s blended structure, anchored by Shell Foundation’s capital, is designed to make that opportunity accessible across the risk-return spectrum. With each transaction, we move a little closer to bridging the financing gap, translating directly into emissions reduced and livelihoods improved.”
For institutional investors, LTEF offers exposure to climate-related assets through a structure designed to distribute risk across different capital providers.
Its performance will depend on credit quality, portfolio growth and measurable environmental and social outcomes.
The fund also provides a potential model for development finance institutions seeking to mobilise commercial capital without relying exclusively on concessional lending.
As emerging economies face growing investment requirements, blended finance structures could help expand access to capital for businesses supporting decarbonisation, employment and economic resilience.

articles.full_text:
Pacific Island Nations Advance 100% Renewable Energy Transition Roadmap
- Pacific Island ministers have discussed a regional roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, advancing a shared vision for 100% renewable energy.
- The initiative builds on the 2023 Port Vila agreement and COP28 commitments, positioning energy security and climate resilience as regional priorities.
- The Asian Development Bank, Beyond Oil & Gas Alliance and NDC Partnership are supporting transition planning, investment pathways and economic resilience.
Pacific Island ministers and regional representatives have advanced discussions on a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, during Pre-COP31 meetings in Fiji.
Developed in partnership with the Beyond Oil & Gas Alliance (BOGA), the initiative centres on a regional vision for 100% renewable energy. It aims to reduce fossil fuel dependence while strengthening economic resilience and energy security across vulnerable island economies.
The discussions follow the establishment of a Pacific Renewable Energy Commissioner at the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in August. That decision created an additional mechanism for coordinating regional energy priorities.
Energy Security Drives Regional Transition Plans
Pacific Island economies face considerable exposure to imported fossil fuels, leaving energy systems vulnerable to international price fluctuations and supply disruptions.
For governments already confronting rising climate adaptation costs, reducing fuel dependence offers both economic and environmental benefits.
Tina Stege, COP31 Pacific envoy and climate envoy for the Marshall Islands, called for accelerated action.
“With climate impacts accelerating, instability rising, economies faltering and the fearsome reality of an overshoot to the 1.5C temperature limit approaching, it’s high time to transition away from fossil fuels,” Stege said.
“The Pacific needs to end its dependency on fossil fuels for our own economic and energy security. We need every region of the globe to follow us in developing a roadmap to a cheaper, cleaner, healthier, secure low-carbon energy future, so we can secure our environmental safety too.”
The proposed roadmap would provide a regional framework for translating political commitments into practical energy transition strategies.
However, implementation will require coordinated investment, stronger electricity infrastructure and financing mechanisms suited to smaller island economies.
Pacific Leadership Builds on Global Climate Commitments
The initiative extends a longstanding regional campaign for stronger international action on fossil fuels.
In 2023, Pacific leaders advanced the Port Vila agreement, calling for a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas production.
Pacific nations also played an influential role in securing the COP28 agreement to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s Minister for Environment and Climate Change, highlighted the region’s continued advocacy.
“The Pacific has, for a long time, spearheaded the transition away from fossil fuels,” Tabuya said.
“From the call in Port Vila three years ago for a fossil-fuel free Pacific, to this year’s Pre-COP hosted in Fiji and Tuvalu, Pacific leaders have advocated tirelessly for a global energy transition. Keeping 1.5 alive is an existential need for us. I’m proud and humbled that Fiji is hosting this event, during which the process for a new, regional roadmap will be discussed. I look forward to the continued results of the Pacific Community’s work.”
The regional process could provide a model for other economies seeking to align energy security with commitments under the Paris Agreement.
RELATED ARTICLE: EcoVadis: APAC Accelerates Past North America in Sustainability Progress
Development Banks Support Investment and Just Transition Planning
Financial and institutional support will be central to converting the roadmap into viable projects.
BOGA and the NDC Partnership have announced support for oil and gas-dependent economies developing transition roadmaps.
Meanwhile, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has established a Just Transition Support Platform for the Pacific.
The platform will help identify investment opportunities and develop feasible transition pathways. Its priorities include energy security, economic development and resilience.
ADB also intends to address the distributional consequences of energy transitions, particularly for vulnerable communities.
“By strengthening the evidence base for policy dialogue and investment planning, we can help ensure that the benefits of transition are widely shared, while potential impacts on vulnerable groups are managed,” said Yevgeniy Zhukov, Director General of ADB’s Climate Change and Sustainable Development Department.
For investors, the regional initiative could help clarify future demand for renewable generation, electricity infrastructure and energy storage.
However, project bankability, financing costs and implementation capacity will remain important considerations.
Regional Roadmap Carries Global Climate Implications
The Pacific initiative places fossil fuel dependence at the centre of regional economic and climate policy.
A coordinated roadmap could help governments establish investment priorities, attract development finance and strengthen accountability for energy transition commitments.
Its significance extends beyond the Pacific. As international negotiations continue over fossil fuel transition pathways, island nations are seeking to demonstrate how regional cooperation can translate global climate commitments into national energy strategies.
The next challenge will be securing the financing and institutional capacity needed to deliver those ambitions.
