articles.full_text:
US SEC Clears BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street in Climate Probe, Warns Investors
- The SEC will not pursue charges against BlackRock, Vanguard or State Street over their involvement in climate-related shareholder activism ahead of ExxonMobil’s 2021 annual meeting.
- Large institutional investors face heightened disclosure scrutiny, as coordinated shareholder engagement could affect their eligibility for simplified ownership reporting.
- The decision raises governance and compliance considerations for asset managers participating in climate initiatives, particularly ahead of the 2027 proxy season.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has decided against charging three of Wall Street’s largest asset managers over climate-related shareholder activism at ExxonMobil.
The decision clears BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street of potential enforcement action linked to the oil company’s contentious 2021 shareholder meeting.
However, the regulator issued a rare Report of Investigation warning that coordinated investor activities could trigger stricter securities disclosure requirements.
The SEC urged major institutional investors to review their regulatory obligations before the 2027 proxy season, particularly when participating in organized shareholder campaigns.
ExxonMobil Vote at Centre of SEC Investigation
The investigation examined investor engagement surrounding ExxonMobil’s 2021 shareholder meeting, when activist hedge fund Engine No. 1 challenged the company’s approach to the energy transition.
Engine No. 1 successfully secured board representation after arguing that ExxonMobil needed stronger oversight of climate-related financial risks.
BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street supported dissident directors during the contest. Climate Action 100+ (CA100+), a global investor initiative focused on corporate climate action, also aligned with Engine No. 1.
The shareholder vote became a defining confrontation over institutional investors’ influence on corporate climate strategy.
The SEC’s investigation examined whether participation in coordinated initiatives could alter investors’ regulatory status under US securities law.
While the three asset managers avoided charges, the regulator’s findings establish potential compliance consequences for similar engagement activities.
SEC Warns of Higher Disclosure Costs
The SEC’s central concern involves the distinction between passive investment ownership and efforts to influence corporate control.
Large asset managers typically use simplified reporting mechanisms when holding substantial stakes without seeking to influence management decisions.
However, coordinated campaigns involving board elections or corporate strategy could affect eligibility for those reporting arrangements.
Such changes may require more extensive ownership disclosures, increasing compliance costs and regulatory exposure.
“Membership in an organization whose stated purpose is to change or influence control of a specific issuer by promoting the election of dissident directors or otherwise could be a factor in the loss of eligibility” to use the cheaper forms, the SEC report states.
The regulator maintained that ordinary shareholder engagement remains permissible.
Jim Moloney, director of the SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance, said the report “reminds asset managers and investors of their responsibilities with respect to shareholder engagement, especially in the context of organized efforts that follow a playbook similar to that of Climate Action 100+. Shareholders have the right to express their views on a particular topic and explain their voting decisions.”
RELATED ARTICLE: US SEC Pauses Climate Disclosure Rule Pending Court Challenge
Political Pressure Reshapes Climate Investor Alliances
The investigation comes amid sustained political opposition to ESG investing in the United States.
Republican lawmakers, particularly those representing energy-producing states, have challenged asset managers over climate commitments and coordinated shareholder activities.
President Donald Trump’s administration has also intensified pressure on companies to retreat from ESG-related policies.
Major investment firms have consequently reassessed their participation in climate alliances.
BlackRock joined CA100+ in 2020 but substantially withdrew in early 2024, citing legal considerations. State Street also exited the initiative, while Vanguard never became a member.
Vanguard separately withdrew from another investment industry climate alliance in 2022, emphasizing its independence.
A 2024 Republican-led congressional investigation revealed concerns within BlackRock and State Street about potential antitrust exposure and reputational risks associated with CA100+ participation.
The SEC’s latest findings also detailed pressure from pension fund members seeking stronger climate engagement from major asset managers.
Implications for Global Asset Managers
Ceres, which coordinates CA100+’s North American activities, defended the initiative’s compliance with securities regulations.
Michael Boudett, Ceres’ general counsel, said the organization operates within US securities law to help investors evaluate climate-related financial risks.
“It is up to every participating Climate Action 100+ investor to make their own decisions, including how they vote their shares,” Boudett said in a statement.
For institutional investors, the SEC’s findings introduce additional considerations when structuring collaborative engagement, exercising voting rights and documenting investment decisions.
The distinction between expressing shareholder views and influencing corporate control will remain central to compliance assessments.
International asset managers with substantial US equity holdings may also need to examine how participation in global climate initiatives interacts with American disclosure rules.
Although enforcement action has been avoided, the SEC’s warning could influence shareholder engagement strategies well beyond the United States.
The outcome leaves investors navigating competing pressures: managing financially material climate risks while ensuring their stewardship activities remain consistent with evolving US securities requirements.

articles.full_text:
LEGO Group Introduces Renewable E-Methanol in Over 90 LEGO Elements
- The LEGO Group has begun using renewable e-methanol to manufacture more than 90 LEGO elements, including connectors, steering wheels and Minifigure hands.
- The material uses renewable energy and captured carbon to produce an alternative to fossil-based feedstocks, supporting lower reliance on virgin fossil resources.
- Five years of supplier collaboration and testing have enabled industrial-scale production, although existing manufacturing processes still incorporate fossil based materials.
The LEGO Group has started using renewable e-methanol in the production of more than 90 LEGO elements, expanding its efforts to reduce reliance on fossil-based plastics.
The Danish toy manufacturer is introducing the material into selected components, including cross axles, connectors, steering wheels and Minifigure hands. The transition follows more than five years of supplier collaboration, testing and manufacturing development.
The initiative forms part of LEGO’s broader strategy to increase renewable and recycled materials across its product portfolio. However, the company must balance environmental objectives with strict requirements for product safety, durability and quality.
Renewable Energy and Captured Carbon Replace Fossil Feedstocks
E-methanol offers an alternative feedstock for plastic production by combining renewable hydrogen with captured carbon.
The manufacturing process, known as Power-to-X, uses renewable electricity to produce hydrogen. This hydrogen then combines with carbon captured from a biogas facility.
Without capture, that carbon would otherwise enter the atmosphere.
The resulting e-methanol can replace a portion of conventional fossil-based inputs used in plastic manufacturing.
Unlike traditional methanol production, which typically relies on fossil fuels, this approach incorporates renewable energy and recovered carbon into the chemical supply chain.
For LEGO, the technology provides another pathway toward reducing dependence on virgin fossil resources without requiring an immediate replacement of existing manufacturing infrastructure.
However, the environmental benefits depend on several factors. These include renewable electricity availability, carbon sourcing, production efficiency and emissions across the material’s lifecycle.
Five Years of Collaboration Enable Industrial Production
The introduction follows a partnership agreement designed to support industrial-scale e-methanol production.
Over five years, LEGO and its suppliers have worked to identify suitable materials, test their performance and integrate renewable feedstocks into established production systems.
The transition has required more than developing an alternative chemical input.
Manufacturers must also ensure that new materials perform consistently within existing production methods while maintaining the structural properties of finished products.
LEGO’s solution involves introducing e-methanol into a continuous production system that also processes virgin fossil-based materials.
This approach allows renewable feedstocks to enter existing manufacturing infrastructure without requiring an immediate transition to exclusively renewable inputs.
It also introduces an important distinction for sustainability reporting.
The use of e-methanol in a shared production system does not necessarily mean individual LEGO elements contain exclusively renewable materials.
Instead, the approach supports a gradual reduction in fossil-based feedstock consumption as renewable material availability expands.
RELATED ARTICLE: The LEGO Group appoints Annette Stube as Chief Sustainability Officer
Scaling Renewable Plastics Across Manufacturing
The development addresses a persistent challenge facing manufacturers seeking to decarbonise plastic-intensive products.
Replacing fossil-based raw materials requires access to commercially viable alternatives that meet established technical specifications.
Even where renewable technologies exist, industrial adoption depends on reliable supply, compatible infrastructure and sufficient production capacity.
LEGO’s experience illustrates the importance of collaboration between manufacturers, chemical producers and renewable energy suppliers.
Such partnerships can help create demand for alternative feedstocks while supporting investment in emerging production technologies.
For corporate sustainability executives, the initiative also raises questions about material traceability, lifecycle emissions and the verification of renewable content.
These considerations become increasingly important as companies face scrutiny over environmental claims and progress toward climate commitments.
Transparent accounting will be essential to distinguish reductions in fossil feedstock consumption from measurable reductions in product-related emissions.
Implications for Global Materials Decarbonisation
LEGO has positioned e-methanol as one component of its wider materials transition rather than a complete replacement for conventional plastics.
The company has not disclosed the volume of e-methanol used or the associated emissions reductions.
Nevertheless, its adoption demonstrates how established manufacturers can begin integrating renewable chemical feedstocks into existing industrial systems.
For investors and corporate leaders, the broader significance lies in the commercial development of renewable materials supply chains.
Scaling these technologies will require sustained investment, reliable renewable electricity and stronger collaboration across industries.
As manufacturers work to reduce Scope 3 emissions, renewable feedstocks could become increasingly relevant to procurement strategies and supplier engagement.
LEGO’s approach provides an example of how industrial partnerships can support that transition while maintaining existing product performance standards.

articles.title: 95% of SMEs Advance on Sustainability, but Only 20% Set Emissions Targets: CDP Report
articles.summary:
Environmental disclosure platform CDP has found that more than 95% of reporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are progressing on environmental management. However, most have yet to translate that preparation […]
The post 95% of SMEs Advance on Sustainability, but Only 20% Set Emissions Targets: CDP Report appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
95% of SMEs Advance on Sustainability, but Only 20% Set Emissions Targets: CDP Report
- More than 95% of nearly 11,000 SMEs assessed by CDP have progressed against at least one environmental indicator, but only 20% have emissions reduction targets.
- 63% of SMEs have or plan to develop a climate transition plan within two years, although just 15% currently have one in place.
- Financial incentives could accelerate supply chain decarbonisation, with CDP research finding suppliers are 52% more likely to reduce annual emissions when buyers offer financial support rather than training alone.
Environmental disclosure platform CDP has found that more than 95% of reporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are progressing on environmental management. However, most have yet to translate that preparation into measurable emissions reductions.
CDP’s SME Disclosure Data Insights 2026 report assessed nearly 11,000 companies using 2025 disclosure data. The analysis examined environmental governance, risk management, transition planning and emissions reduction efforts.
SMEs account for approximately 90% of businesses worldwide and 60% of global business-related emissions. Their ability to decarbonise is therefore critical to corporate climate commitments and wider supply chain sustainability.
While nearly 40% of disclosing SMEs meet most or all basic environmental indicators, significant implementation gaps remain. Only 20% have established emissions reduction targets, while 32% have reduction initiatives underway.
Transition Planning Advances, but Implementation Lags
CDP’s findings reveal growing interest in formal climate transition planning.
Approximately 63% of SMEs either have a transition plan or expect to establish one within two years. Yet only 15% currently have a plan in place.
The figures suggest companies are strengthening environmental governance before committing resources to operational changes.
Progress in risk management, stakeholder engagement and internal oversight provides a foundation for future emissions reductions. However, these measures alone cannot deliver the decarbonisation required across global value chains.
Simon Fischweicher, CDP Chief Customer Success Officer, said: “SMEs are indispensable to the transition to a net-zero, earth-positive economy. Our data shows that many are already doing the hard work of putting the foundations in place by understanding environmental risks, strengthening governance and preparing for transition. But foundations alone will not cut emissions. The next step is helping SMEs turn preparation into progress: setting and achieving credible targets, investing in emissions reduction initiatives and embedding action throughout their businesses. Buyers, financial institutions and policymakers have an important role to play by making finance, incentives and practical support more accessible; helping SMEs strengthen their resilience and competitiveness while accelerating the transition.”
European SMEs Lead Environmental Disclosure Progress
Regional performance varies considerably, reflecting differences in market expectations, reporting practices and regulatory environments.
European SMEs demonstrate some of the strongest results, with Spain, France and Sweden leading among the countries assessed.
Their performance comes as Europe develops more standardised sustainability reporting approaches for smaller businesses.
The Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for SMEs (VSME) provides a framework for companies responding to environmental information requests from customers and financial institutions.
RELATED ARTICLE: CDP Names Beth Thoren as CEO to Lead New Foundation
CDP’s dedicated SME questionnaire aligns closely with European reporting frameworks, including VSME.
By comparison, SMEs in Singapore and the United States recorded the weakest performance. Most companies assessed in these markets met few or none of CDP’s basic indicators.
The regional differences highlight the importance of accessible reporting frameworks and consistent sustainability expectations across supply chains.
Financial Incentives Could Accelerate Supply Chain Decarbonisation
CDP’s analysis also identifies substantial differences between industries.
SMEs operating in manufacturing, materials, transportation services and power generation demonstrate some of the strongest progress against basic environmental indicators.
These sectors play important roles in industrial decarbonisation because of their emissions profiles and dependencies on natural resources.
Retail and services companies recorded comparatively weaker performance, creating potential challenges for businesses seeking comprehensive value chain emissions reductions.
Financing remains another critical consideration.
Previous CDP research conducted with HSBC found suppliers were 52% more likely to reduce annual emissions when buyers offered financial incentives compared with training alone.
The findings suggest corporate procurement strategies can influence environmental outcomes beyond direct operations.
For multinational companies, supporting smaller suppliers through financing, incentives and practical assistance could strengthen progress against Scope 3 emissions targets.
Financial institutions also have an opportunity to connect sustainability-linked support with credible transition planning and measurable environmental improvements.
For policymakers, the challenge extends beyond expanding disclosure requirements. Smaller businesses also need the resources and incentives to implement the changes identified through reporting.
CDP’s findings illustrate a central challenge for global decarbonisation: environmental disclosure is becoming more established among participating SMEs, but implementation remains limited.
Closing that gap will require stronger coordination between businesses, investors and governments, particularly as corporate climate commitments increasingly depend on emissions reductions throughout global supply chains.

articles.summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy is preparing to provide up to $4.2 billion in financing for upgrades to Vistra’s nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio. The investment targets existing reactors […]
The post DOE Backs Vistra Nuclear Upgrades With $4.2 Billion Loan Commitment appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
DOE Backs Vistra Nuclear Upgrades With $4.2 Billion Loan Commitment
- The U.S. Department of Energy has conditionally committed up to $4.2 billion to nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra’s fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio.
- The projects are expected to preserve nearly 4 GW of existing nuclear generation and add 433 MW of new capacity across the PJM power market.
- Vistra plans to extend operations at three nuclear plants by another 20 years beyond their existing licenses, while supporting about 3,000 project-related jobs.
The U.S. Department of Energy is preparing to provide up to $4.2 billion in financing for upgrades to Vistra’s nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio. The investment targets existing reactors as electricity demand rises across one of America’s largest power markets.
The conditional loan commitment comes from the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing. It will support nuclear uprates and modernization at Vistra facilities serving the PJM Interconnection.
The projects could preserve nearly 4 GW of baseload generation, enough to power more than 3 million homes. They are also expected to add 433 MW of nuclear capacity without requiring equivalent new generation resources or transmission corridors.
“President Trump promised to unleash an American nuclear renaissance, and the Energy Department is delivering,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, around-the-clock energy for American families and businesses.”
Existing reactors become a capacity strategy
Vistra plans investments at the Beaver Valley nuclear plant in Pennsylvania and the Davis-Besse and Perry facilities in Ohio.
Rather than building reactors from scratch, the projects aim to extract additional electricity from existing nuclear assets. They would also support plant operations for an additional 20 years beyond their current licenses.
That approach is gaining relevance as utilities and policymakers confront rising power demand alongside lengthy timelines for new generation and transmission infrastructure.
The financing advances President Donald Trump’s Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base. The administration has positioned nuclear energy as a central part of its strategy for energy security, grid reliability and domestic industrial growth.
“President Trump and Secretary Wright have set a clear direction for America’s nuclear future, and EDF is financing the projects that advance that mission,” said EDF Director Gregory A. Beard. “These investments will extend the life of existing reactors, increase nuclear generation, and deliver abundant, around-the-clock power to lower costs and power American prosperity for decades to come.”
RELATED ARTICLE: U.S. Department of the Treasury, IRS Release Final Rules to Ensure Good-Paying Clean Energy Jobs, Expand Clean Energy Workforce
PJM demand puts firm power in focus
The investment has implications beyond the three plants.
PJM spans 13 states and faces growing pressure to secure enough generation as electricity consumption increases. Nuclear plants offer around-the-clock generation without the direct carbon emissions associated with fossil fuel power.
For companies with expanding electricity requirements, including data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities, maintaining existing nuclear capacity can also reduce exposure to power supply constraints.
DOE estimates the projects will support about 3,000 jobs tied to engineering, construction and planned outage work. Thousands of permanent positions associated with the plants would also be preserved.
The conditional commitment contains another potential expansion. DOE could finance future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas, extending the financing strategy beyond PJM.
Financing remains conditional
The $4.2 billion commitment is not yet a finalized loan.
Vistra must meet technical, legal, environmental and financial requirements before DOE enters definitive financing agreements or releases funding. That process leaves execution, regulatory and project risks in place.
For investors and corporate energy buyers, however, the proposed financing illustrates how U.S. energy policy is shifting toward maximizing existing nuclear infrastructure.
Extending reactor lives and increasing output can add firm generation faster than developing entirely new nuclear facilities. It can also preserve large volumes of carbon-free electricity already embedded in regional grids.
If completed as planned, the Pennsylvania and Ohio investments will keep almost 4 GW of nuclear generation operating while adding hundreds of megawatts of new capacity. Their broader importance lies in how the U.S. finances the next phase of power demand: not only through new projects, but by extracting more value from infrastructure already on the grid.

articles.full_text:
NFWF Launches $18 Million Fund to Protect US Great Plains Grasslands
- $18 million in initial funding from the Walmart Foundation, McDonald’s USA and its suppliers will support grassland conservation across the US Great Plains.
- Up to 400,000 acres targeted: The fund aims to permanently protect 150,000 to 200,000 acres while improving regenerative management across another 150,000 to 200,000 acres.
- $10 million in initial grants will support rancher-led conservation, wildlife habitat protection and agricultural supply chain resilience, with first awards expected in 2027.
The National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) has launched an $18 million conservation fund to protect grasslands across the US Great Plains. The initiative brings together major food retailers, agricultural suppliers and philanthropic capital to address land conversion and ecosystem degradation.
The Great Plains Grassland Fund will support permanent land conservation and regenerative ranching practices across one of North America’s most important agricultural regions.
An initial $9 million grant from the Walmart Foundation will be matched by $9 million in aligned funding from McDonald’s USA and several of its primary beef and beverage suppliers.
The public-private initiative aims to protect biodiversity while strengthening the long-term resilience of agricultural supply chains that depend on healthy grassland ecosystems.
Targeting Grassland Conversion and Agricultural Resilience
The Great Plains contain extensive working ranchlands that support livestock production, wildlife habitats and regional water systems.
However, grassland conversion and land degradation create growing challenges for conservation and agricultural productivity.
NFWF’s new fund will address these pressures through voluntary conservation agreements and technical support for ranching operations.
A central objective is to secure permanent conservation easements across 150,000 to 200,000 acres of high-value grasslands facing conversion risks.
These agreements will help prevent future land conversion while allowing participating landowners to maintain compatible agricultural activities.
The initiative also targets regenerative management improvements across an additional 150,000 to 200,000 acres of working ranchlands.
Participating ranchers will receive technical assistance to adopt practices that improve soil health, strengthen ecosystem resilience and support sustainable livestock production.
Beyond agricultural land management, the programme will prioritise wildlife migration corridors and watershed protection.
These measures aim to preserve ecological connectivity while supporting water quality and rural communities.
Walmart and McDonald’s Mobilise Conservation Capital
The fund’s financing structure combines philanthropic investment with contributions from businesses directly exposed to agricultural supply chain risks.
The Walmart Foundation’s $9 million commitment provides half of the initial capital.
McDonald’s USA and participating beef and beverage suppliers will contribute the remaining $9 million.
Their involvement connects conservation financing with industries that rely on productive ranchlands and stable agricultural ecosystems.
For food companies, grassland degradation can create long-term operational risks through declining soil productivity, water pressures and disruptions to livestock supply chains.
Supporting conservation across working agricultural landscapes offers a way to address these risks beyond individual corporate operations.
Jeff Trandahl, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer of NFWF, described the initiative as a scalable framework for public and private partners to support rancher-led conservation.
Julie Gehrki, Senior Vice President at Walmart and President of the Walmart Foundation, Cesar Piña, Senior Vice President and Chief Supply Chain Officer for North America at McDonald’s USA, also emphasised the importance of cross-industry collaboration.
Their organisations view coordinated investment as essential to strengthening agricultural resilience and supporting rural economies.
RELATED ARTICLE: McDonald’s USA Commits $200 M to Regenerative Ranching Across 38 States
$10 Million Grant Programme Opens Path to Implementation
NFWF plans to launch an initial competitive Request for Proposals offering up to $10 million in project grants.
The first funding awards are scheduled for announcement in 2027.
Eligible conservation activities will focus on protecting intact grasslands, improving ranchland management and preserving critical habitats.
The programme’s voluntary approach places ranchers and landowners at the centre of implementation.
Rather than removing agricultural land from production, the fund seeks to integrate conservation objectives with economically viable ranching operations.
This structure could help participating businesses direct capital toward measurable land management outcomes while maintaining productive agricultural landscapes.
Implications for Corporate Nature and Supply Chain Strategies
The initiative reflects growing corporate attention to biodiversity, land use and nature-related supply chain exposure.
For food and agricultural companies, environmental risks increasingly extend beyond direct emissions to the condition of ecosystems supporting production.
Conservation easements provide a mechanism for long-term land protection, while regenerative management programmes can support improvements across active agricultural operations.
However, the fund’s eventual impact will depend on implementation, landowner participation and measurable conservation outcomes.
For investors and corporate sustainability leaders, the programme offers an example of shared financing for environmental risks that extend across multiple supply chains.
Its relevance also extends beyond the United States. Agricultural regions worldwide face similar pressures from land conversion, biodiversity loss and resource degradation.
The Great Plains Grassland Fund will test how coordinated corporate and philanthropic investment can support conservation while maintaining the economic foundations of agricultural communities.
